report:

Overall outcome                             The school is likely to meet the relevant
                                            independent school standards if the
                                            material change is implemented

This inspection was commissioned by the Department for Education (DfE), which
is the registration authority for independent schools. The school has applied to the
DfE to make a material change to its registration. The school proposes to change
the maximum number of pupils attending.

The purpose of the inspection is to advise the Secretary of State for Education
about the school's compliance with the independent school standards that are
relevant to the material change that the school has applied to make.


Part 8. Quality of leadership in and management of schools
When we carry out material change inspections of independent schools, we report
on the school's likely compliance with part 8 of the independent school standards
first. Under part 8, the proprietor is required to ensure that the school meets all of
the independent school standards (the standards) consistently. The standard in
part 8 is intended to ensure that the quality of leadership and management at the
school is sufficient for that purpose.

All leaders, including the proprietor and governors are passionate about providing
a nurturing, high-quality education for the pupils this school serves. The proprietor
understands the requirements of the standards in full. The school has clear, robust
systems in place to ensure that the standards continue to be met. The proprietor
has an appropriately staffed and qualified central team which supports school
leaders to maintain oversight of the standards. The school governing body
provides the proprietor with robust challenge about how well the standards
continue to be met.


New Forest School, 2 July 2026
                                                                                     1
 Leaders demonstrate secure knowledge and skills appropriate to their roles. The
school has a well-qualified and suitably experienced senior leadership team which
has oversight of all the school sites. This team includes the school’s designated
safeguarding lead. In addition, senior leaders based at each site oversee day-to-
day management and safeguarding at their specific site.

There is a clear rationale for the proposed material change request. The proposed
increase in pupil numbers will meet a local area need for additional special school
places. The proprietor intends to maintain low pupil numbers at each of the school
sites with the proposed increase in pupil numbers to be across the sites. They
have determined the maximum number of pupils they intend to educate at each
site. This ranges from 34 to 48 pupils. The total number of pupils across all sites
will be 150. There is no intention currently to increase the number of sites the
school has.

The proprietor has made sure that the school’s accommodation and facilities are at
least sufficient to support the proposed increase in pupil numbers. The school has
ample space across the 4 sites to house the additional pupils. Leaders’ proposed
capacity for each site is sensible and well considered. Capacity at each site is
perfectly adequate for the proposed numbers and the furniture and staffing to
enable this capacity to be met is already in place.

The proprietor has carefully considered the impact of the proposed material
change on the staff and pupils in the school. The proprietor intends to increase the
number of pupils on each site up to the maximum identified capacity slowly. This is
to minimise the disruption to the existing pupil population. Leaders are determined
that any additional pupils added to class groups should fit in well with those
already attending the school.

The proprietor intends that class groups will not contain more than 4 pupils. Each
group will be taught by a qualified teacher and have a teaching assistant.
Currently, the school has sufficient teaching staff to support the increase in pupil
numbers while maintaining a maximum class size of 4 pupils. However, leaders
intend to continue to expand the capacity of support staff and pastoral staff on
some sites.

Leaders have taken appropriate steps to actively promote the wellbeing of the
pupils. Designated safeguarding leaders work closely with staff to ensure a strong
culture of vigilance that keeps pupils safe. In addition, expert pastoral teams
provide wellbeing support for pupils at each site. Furthermore, the proprietor
employs a team of specialist staff who provide a range of therapy services across
the school.

The standards in this part are likely to be met if the proposed material change is
approved.

 Part 3. Welfare, health and safety of pupils
Safeguarding

The school has a positive safeguarding culture. Leaders understand their
safeguarding responsibilities well. The proprietor has ensured sufficient,
appropriately qualified safeguarding leaders at each of the school sites. In
addition, the school’s headteacher maintains close oversight of safeguarding
across the whole school. A suitable policy detailing the school’s safeguarding
arrangements is published on the school’s website.

The school’s safeguarding and safer-recruitment policies are up to date and
comply with current statutory guidance. A carefully designed programme of
regular training ensures that staff understand their safeguarding responsibilities
well. This keeps safeguarding high on the school’s agenda.

Safeguarding leaders prioritise the welfare, health and safety of pupils and staff.
Staff know how to recognise when pupils may be at risk of harm. They understand
how to refer any concerns they may have and how to assure themselves that
appropriate action has been taken. The school has secure systems in place to
record and escalate safeguarding concerns. Leaders take appropriate steps to get
pupils the help that they need when at risk of harm.

Pupils are happy, confident and feel safe. They are keen to come into school and
be ready to learn. Pupils’ positive manner, presentation and behaviour
demonstrates that they feel safe and secure.

Supervision of pupils

Across the school, leaders ensure high levels of supervision. Pupils are supervised
appropriately throughout the school day, including when they are moving around
the buildings and when they are using the outdoor areas. The staff-to-pupil ratio
of 2 adults to 4 pupils is often exceeded. This provides additional capacity to
accommodate the proposed increase in pupil numbers without the need to employ
a substantial additional number of staff. The proprietor has employed well-
qualified staff who take good care of pupils.

Health and safety and fire

Leaders have written a comprehensive health and safety policy. This is available on
the school website. It ensures that the school complies with relevant health and
safety laws. Leaders make appropriate checks for the health and safety of the
school site. The proprietor employs a wide range of maintenance staff to carry out



New Forest School, 2 July 2026
                                                                                     3
 these checks and make any necessary repairs. Leaders have an accurate oversight
of the checks and respond rapidly where any actions are needed.

Fire safety compliance is robust. The school complies fully with the Regulatory
Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005. Each site displays clear fire signage. This
includes signs to show the locations of fire exits, evacuation routes and fire
assembly points. Leaders ensure that fire equipment is checked regularly. These
checks are recorded in detail. In addition, records show that all fire equipment is
inspected as required. The proprietor ensures fire safety risk assessments are
carried out frequently and any issues rectified swiftly.

Fire extinguishers are appropriately located and well maintained. They are
accessible to staff.

Risk assessment

There is a robust risk assessment policy in place. Leaders have produced a wide
range of appropriate written risk assessments. Risk assessments for specific
activities and components of the different sites are thorough and show a careful
consideration of risks with appropriate mitigations. Individual pupil risk
assessments are also sufficiently detailed. Leaders update these regularly in line
with pupils’ changing needs.

The independent school standards in this part are likely to be met if the proposed
material change is approved.


Part 4. Suitability of staff, supply staff, and proprietors
The recruitment checks made on staff, supply staff and the proprietor

Leaders understand the checks they need to make to ensure that adults are safe
to work with pupils. The proprietor employs a centrally based human resources
team to oversee recruitment and the onboarding of new staff. They carry out all
appropriate checks on new members of staff prior to them beginning work at the
school. This process is checked by suitably qualified senior leaders to ensure that
it complies with the most up-to-date statutory requirements. This ensures that
adults are safe to work with children.

The school’s safer recruitment policy provides detailed information on safer
recruitment process and sets out clear roles and responsibilities.

The single central record of these recruitment checks

 The school maintains an appropriate single central record of the recruitment
checks. This record contains all the necessary evidence of the different checks the
school has completed.

The standards in this part are likely to be met if the proposed material change is
approved.


Part 5. Premises of and accommodation at schools
Toilet and washing facilities, water supply, changing accommodation
and showers

On every site the school has suitable toilet facilities with hot and cold running
water. These are all lockable from the inside and only for use by one person at a
time. The temperature of the hot water is regulated appropriately. It does not
pose a scalding risk.

At each site, drinking water is provided from clearly marked sinks. Pupils can
access drinking water at all times. These are separate from toilet facilities as
required.

At each site that has secondary-aged pupils, there is suitable changing
accommodation and a shower for pupils to use, if needed.

Medical room and accommodation for pupils' therapy needs

Each school site has a suitable space for use as a medical room. On 3 sites, there
is a dedicated medical room and at the other sites there is a suitable and
appropriately equipped space. All medical spaces are located near to changing
facilities, running water and a toilet. The school’s medical facilities provide
comfortable spaces for the short-term care of sick and injured pupils. All staff have
appropriate first aid training.

Ensuring the health, safety and welfare of pupils

Each school site is well maintained. All buildings are maintained to a suitably high
standard. The accommodation is very well decorated and furnished appropriately
to meet the needs of the pupils. The school’s classrooms are mostly large and airy
and provide ample space for the proposed number of pupils the school intends to
accommodate.

All learning spaces have an appropriately wide range of resources to support
pupils’ learning. Each school site also has a range of additional specialist learning
rooms for subjects such as music, computing, art, science and design technology.



New Forest School, 2 July 2026
                                                                                     5
 In all specialist classrooms, leaders have taken suitable steps to mitigate any
additional risks, such as accidents from using specialist equipment and chemicals.
All dangerous items are safely locked away and only used with appropriate adult
supervision.

Each school site also includes smaller spaces for use as breakout rooms for
individual and small-group interventions and therapeutic support. All spaces are
well resourced and fit for purpose.

The school’s outdoor learning centre is set in extensive grounds in a rural location.
Classrooms are housed in former barns which have been refurbished to a high
standard. Pupils also benefit from additional outdoor activities such as climbing
and archery. These are located in purposely designed indoor spaces with
appropriate, high-quality specialist resources. In addition, pupils have access to
animal care facilities and an extensive woodland area.

Leaders have established effective systems to check the accommodation regularly
for wear and tear. Suitably qualified maintenance staff are readily available to carry
out any necessary repairs so that the school buildings continue to be well
maintained.

Lighting and acoustic conditions

At each site, the classrooms and other indoor spaces are large, bright and airy.
They have suitable lighting. Leaders have ensured that the acoustic conditions are
appropriate and suitable for the additional needs of the pupils.

There is ample external lighting around the school site to ensure the safety of
pupils and staff when it is dark. External lighting is provided at all sites and is
tested regularly.

Outdoor space

Each of the school sites has suitable outdoor space for the pupils to use for play
and physical education. In addition, the outdoor learning centre has specialist
indoor facilities for climbing and archery and access to extensive grounds and a
woodland area for forest-based activities. Pupils also benefit from regular sessions
at the school farm which provide opportunities to learn and take part in outdoor
physical activity.

At each site there are well-maintained outdoor areas which provide comfortable
spaces for pupils to sit, eat and talk to their friends.

The standards in this part are likely to be met if the proposed material change is
approved.

 The school's accessibility plan
The proprietor has ensured that the school complies with the requirements of the
Equality Act 2010. There is a suitable accessibility plan for the school.

Inspectors carried out this inspection under section 162(4) of the Education Act
2002, at the request of the registration authority for independent schools.
Inspectors checked the school's likely compliance with the independent school
standards. These are the requirements set out in the schedule to the Education
(Independent School Standards) Regulations 2014.

Following our updated inspection framework, all inspections are now led by
His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMI) or by Ofsted Inspectors (OIs) who have
previously served as HMIs.

The inspector spoke with the chair of proprietors and the chair of governors, the
executive headteacher, the headteacher and other school leaders during the
inspection.

The inspector confirmed the following information about the school:

New Forest School is part of New Forest Care, a group which also runs several
children’s homes. The group provides residential, educational and therapeutic
provision across its providers.

The school is a split-school site comprising four main sites and a farm. Fawley is
the ‘home site’ and the others include:
Dibden site, Lundale Road, Dibden Purlieu, Hampshire SO45 4QN
Totton site, Water Lane, Totton, Hampshire SO40 3ZX
The Outdoor Learning Centre, Romsey, Hampshire SO51 6AB
Bartley Forest Farm, Old Lyndhurst Road, Cadnam, Hampshire SO40 2NR

All pupils who attend have an EHC plan and a diagnosis of autism or social,
emotional and/or mental health needs. Many pupils are in the care of a local
authority.

The school is not currently using any alternative provision.

Material change inspection                  3 June 2026
report:

Overall outcome                             The school is likely to meet the relevant
                                            independent school standards if the
                                            material changes relating to the school
                                            provision are implemented

This inspection was commissioned by the Department for Education (DfE), which
is the registration authority for independent schools. The school has applied to the
DfE to make a material change to its registration. The school proposes to change
the age range of pupils and increase the maximum number of pupils attending.

The purpose of the inspection is to advise the Secretary of State for Education
about the school’s likely compliance with the independent school standards that
are relevant to the material change that the school has applied to make.


Part 8. Quality of leadership in and management of schools
When we carry out material change inspections of independent schools, we report
on the school’s likely compliance with part 8 of the independent school standards
first. Under part 8, the proprietor is required to ensure that the school meets all of
the independent school standards consistently. The standard in part 8 is intended
to ensure that the quality of leadership and management at the school is sufficient
for that purpose.

Leadership across the school is effective. The headteacher, who also operates as
the proprietor, and other leaders bring relevant expertise to their roles. They forge
meaningful connections with other professional networks, such as being part of
local working groups with other independent schools. Leaders also utilise an
Executive Board, who have significant and broad ranging educational and wider
expertise. This expertise is brought to bear to further develop the provision and
offer support and challenge to leaders.


Yew Tree Farm School, 3 June 2026
                                                                                    1
 Current pupils are happy and feel safe and secure. They trust staff and develop
positive relationships rapidly. High staff ratios mean that pupils are supported to
develop and maintain effective relationships through tailored support. Staff receive
appropriate training so that they can undertake their roles effectively.

Leaders have made significant developments to the school site to ensure that
there is sufficient space and resources for the proposed additional pupil numbers
to be educated, including creating additional classrooms. Careful thought has been
given to designing a curriculum that meets the needs of the proposed secondary-
age pupils that leaders wish to cater for. Leaders are planning sensibly to grow
their provision steadily over time so as to maintain the quality of their provision.

Leaders demonstrate a secure understanding of the independent school standards
and take actions to ensure that they are readily met. They are, therefore, likely to
meet these if the material change application is approved.


Part 1. Quality of education provided
Curriculum, teaching and assessment

Leaders have developed an appropriate curriculum offer for the proposed
secondary-age pupils they plan to cater for. This builds effectively on the
foundations of their primary curriculum, and is likely to meet pupils’ specific special
educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND). Pupils all receive English and
mathematics teaching in one-to-one lessons, and access a wider curriculum offer
in small groups, which is built around their needs and aptitudes. This is
established in the primary phase and intended to continue in the secondary phase
should the material change be approved. There are appropriate plans in place for
pupils to receive careers advice and guidance, tailored to their individual needs, as
well as an appropriate programme for personal, social, health, relationships and
economic education.

Leaders ensure that staff are well trained to deliver the curriculum and adapt
lessons to ensure that pupils’ additional needs are met effectively. Careful
monitoring of pupil progress ensures that staff and leaders can track pupils’
progress, both through the curriculum and against their individualised targets from
education, health and care plans.

Therefore, the standards are likely to be met if the material change is approved.

                                                                                     2
 Part 2. Spiritual, moral, social and cultural development of
pupils
Leaders place an effective emphasis on pupils’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural
development for current pupils, and intend to do the same for pupils up to the age
of 16. Opportunities will be woven through the curriculum for pupils to learn to
work collaboratively with others and to develop their confidence, resilience and
increasing independence. Leaders intend that positive relationships with staff who
model these traits will support pupils with SEND to develop these essential skills
into the secondary phase.

Leaders intend to maintain an appropriate focus on developing social and
emotional resilience that is tailored around pupils’ individual needs. This will
include bespoke approaches with specialists as needed. Older pupils will learn how
to develop positive and healthy relationships with others as part of an
appropriately planned curriculum. Extra-curricular opportunities are likely to be
well considered to develop pupils’ experience and confidence in the wider world as
they progress into the secondary phase.

Leaders have planned programmes to ensure that their well-established provision
for primary-age pupils is built upon and develops so that it is suitable for the
secondary-age pupils they wish to cater for. Therefore, the standards in this part
are likely to be met if the material change is approved.


Part 3. Welfare, health and safety of pupils
Safeguarding

The school’s ‘child protection and safeguarding policy’ is aligned with statutory
requirements and published on the school’s website. Staff receive regular and
comprehensive safeguarding training. This ensures they can identify when a pupil
may be at risk of harm and report any concerns swiftly. Leaders intend to train
staff in the potential safeguarding risks for pupils of secondary age. They have
made appropriate consideration in risk assessments for mixed age teaching, which
will include secondary-age pupils.

Leaders are appropriately trained for their role in overseeing the safeguarding
culture in their school. This includes 2 senior leaders, who have appropriate
training to perform the role of designated safeguarding lead. They work well with
external agencies so that pupils and their families receive appropriate and timely
support. Records are kept of actions undertaken, which are appropriately detailed
and demonstrate that responses are timely.




Yew Tree Farm School, 3 June 2026
                                                                                  3
 Pupils feel safe, have positive relationships with staff and are confident to share
any worries they have. They know who they would speak to if they have any
concerns.

Health and safety, fire and first aid

The school has appropriate health and safety and first-aid policies in place that
support the welfare of pupils and staff. These policies are implemented
consistently and underpinned by effective systems. Leaders ensure that frequent
health and safety checks of the school site are carried out. Any identified
issues are addressed swiftly. As a result of these systems, the site is maintained to
a high standard and is safe.

A compliant fire safety policy is in place. Clear escape routes are supported by
ample signage. Robust systems, including frequent checks of alarms, fire
extinguishers and emergency lighting are in place. Regular external checks are
undertaken of fire extinguishers to ensure these are well maintained. These
processes ensure the school maintains ongoing compliance with fire safety
regulations.

Risk assessment

A thorough risk assessment policy is in place, supported by clear systems and
processes that are carefully followed. Risk assessments are well written, reflecting
the specific needs of pupils and the activities they undertake. This includes for the
site-based use of tools, working with animals on the farm, as well as off-site visits,
such as trips.

Leaders have individual risk assessments in place that are reviewed frequently to
ensure they are appropriate to pupils’ needs. These risk assessments are similarly
detailed, identifying pupils’ vulnerabilities and any associated risks. These plans
clearly set out appropriate mitigating actions to reduce potential risk, meaning that
they remain responsive to pupils’ ongoing needs and circumstances.

Leaders have carefully considered the demands of increasing the number of pupils
on the school site and have made effective provision for this. There has been
careful identification of the potential risks posed, for example, for mixed age
groups on the school site, which is pertinent given the request to increase the age
range of pupils to span both primary- and secondary-age pupils. As a result, the
proprietor body has ensured that the standards in this part are likely to be met.

 Part 4. Suitability of staff, supply staff, and proprietors
The recruitment checks made on staff, supply staff and the proprietor

The school’s recruitment processes are robust and give due regard to safer
recruitment requirements. The senior leaders involved in recruitment are
appropriately trained.

The school has plans to recruit additional staff to meet the needs of the proposed
increased capacity, who they will train to deliver the curriculum. They have
appropriate training and monitoring programmes in place to ensure that all new
staff are able to support pupils safely and effectively.

The single central record of these recruitment checks

The single central record (SCR) is accurately maintained, kept up to date and
includes all staff. The proprietor and executive board representatives check the
SCR regularly to ensure that it reflects the most recent statutory guidance. All
required checks, including those for individuals in leadership and management
roles, are completed and recorded appropriately.

The proprietor has ensured that the standards in this part are likely to be met.


Part 5. Premises of and accommodation at schools
Toilet and washing facilities, water supply, changing accommodation
and showers

The school site has appropriate toilets and handwashing facilities for pupils that
are separate from staff amenities. Showers are accessed at the local leisure
centre, where physical education lessons are undertaken.

Hot water is set at a safe temperature and is regularly checked. Pupils have access
to drinking water throughout the school day, which is clearly labelled.

Medical room and accommodation for pupils’ therapy needs

An on-site medical room is appropriately located next to a toilet and handwashing
facilities are readily available. The room contains a fold out bed and suitable first-
aid provisions, as well as an emergency eye-wash station. Medication is stored
securely in locked facilities.




Yew Tree Farm School, 3 June 2026
                                                                                     5
 Ensuring the health, safety and welfare of pupils

The premises provide a safe and well-resourced environment that is effectively
maintained. Leaders have created an appropriate site comprising 3 additional
classroom learning areas to serve the additional proposed pupil numbers, as well
as break out spaces. A fire-pit is well maintained and appropriately risk assessed
so that this can be used safely and comprises a central element of the school day.
Outside areas, such as ‘the copse’, are also well maintained and accessed by
pupils, when they need to regulate their behaviour. These too are appropriately
risk assessed and used under supervision of staff.

Staffing levels are appropriate and staff are well trained so that they supervise
pupils effectively throughout the day. The school has plans to
recruit additional staff to meet the needs of the proposed increased capacity, who
they will train to deliver the bespoke curriculum. They have appropriate
consideration for high staff to pupil ratios in anticipation of pupils’ SEND needs.
They have well-considered induction and training programmes in place to ensure
that all new staff are able to support pupils safely and confidently.

Lighting and acoustic conditions

Learning spaces, including communal areas, have appropriate acoustic conditions
and suitable internal lighting that support effective teaching and learning. External
lighting is appropriate, contributing to a safe and sufficiently illuminated
environment.

Outdoor space

The external school grounds are well maintained and provide adequate space for
physical education, although most physical education lessons are accessed at a
local leisure centre. Leaders have ensured that the outdoor areas allow pupils to
socialise safely during breaktimes and lunchtimes. These are managed well and
supervised so that pupils can use them safely. The space is suitable to be used by
secondary-age pupils with SEND. There is enough space to accommodate the
extra pupils the school intends to admit.

Leaders have ensured that the standards in this part are likely to be met were the
material change to be approved.

The purpose of this inspection was to advise the Secretary of State for Education
about the proposed school’s likely compliance with the independent school
standards and associated requirements that are required for registration as an
independent school.

Part 8. Quality of leadership in and management of schools
When we carry out progress monitoring inspections of independent schools, we report on
the school’s likely compliance with part 8 of the independent school standards first. Under
part 8, the proprietor is required to ensure that the school meets all of the independent
school standards consistently. The standard in part 8 is intended to ensure that the quality
of leadership and management at the school is sufficient for that purpose.

The proprietor has not taken sufficient action to address the independent school standards
(the standards) that were unmet at the last standard inspection. The action plan that the
proprietor submitted following the inspection was rejected by the Department for
Education. The proprietor does not demonstrate sufficient understanding of how to meet
the standards consistently. Over time, the school’s ability to meet the standards has
fluctuated. During this inspection, multiple standards that were met at the last inspection
were found to be now unmet.

The proprietor has not established the required systems and processes to ensure that
pupils are safe in the school. For example, visitors’ identity is not checked on arrival, nor
are visitors routinely required to sign in. The proprietor does not ensure that the school
has sufficient leadership capacity to bring about the improvements required. Staff do not


Inspection report: Froebel House School, 11 March 2026

 receive any subject-specific training, or sufficient time, to enable them to fulfil their roles
effectively. For example, the school has not trained staff in how to support pupils with
special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND) or other barriers to learning and/or
wellbeing. This means that the school does not meet these pupils’ needs effectively.
The proprietor’s arrangements to meet schedule 10 of the Equality Act 2019 are not
sufficient.

The proprietor has not ensured that the standards in this part are met.


Part 1. Quality of education provided
Curriculum and teaching

Pupils study a broad curriculum. In some subjects, such as art and design and personal,
social and health education (PSHE), the curriculum is suitably structured and organised. In
other subjects, leaders have not ensured that the curriculum is coherently sequenced and
progressive so that pupils’ knowledge builds over time. Where the curriculum is sequenced
effectively, pupils can talk about their learning. For example, they know they have learned
about puberty in PSHE.

The proprietor does not have sufficient knowledge of the early years foundation stage
curriculum to ensure that all requirements are met. Consequently, the prime area of
physical development is not prioritised as it should be. Children in the early years have
limited access to high-quality outdoor provision. This inhibits the development of
important skills, such as their gross motor skills.

The proprietor does not provide subject leaders with sufficient time or training to fulfil
their roles effectively. This limits their ability to complete the monitoring activities set out
in the monitoring cycle. As such, subject leaders do not have a clear view of the quality of
curriculum implementation and where improvements are needed.

The curriculum does not take into account the aptitudes and needs of all pupils. Staff do
not receive training to help them to teach the curriculum well. Consequently, they do not
know, for example, how to adapt lessons to meet the needs of pupils with SEND or other
barriers to their learning, such as speaking English as an additional language. Leaders do
not have sufficient knowledge of SEND to ensure staff are supported with this area of their
work. The information that the school holds about pupils with SEND is out of date. Some
pupils who should be recorded on the SEND register are not. This means that these pupils
do not receive the consideration for their needs that they should. The proprietor is not
aware of their obligation to apply for an education, health and care plan where this would
be of benefit to a pupil.

The school’s approach to behaviour management does not prepare pupils effectively for
the responsibilities of life in British society. The school does not encourage pupils to take
responsibility for their actions, instead following a more punitive approach. For example,

 leaders removed equipment from the playground because pupils did not use it
appropriately. They did not educate pupils about its proper use.
Some pupils demonstrate knowledge of fundamental British values and different faiths.

Assessment

The school has recently purchased summative assessments for English and mathematics.
The outcomes of these assessments will be used to inform pupil progress meetings, but
this framework for assessment is not well established or embedded.

The proprietor has not ensured that the standards in this part are met.


Part 2. Spiritual, moral, social and cultural development of pupils
The school’s approach to behaviour inhibits the development of pupils’ self-esteem and
self-confidence. Some pupils do not enjoy attending school. Pupils describe hearing their
peers using derogatory, including racist, language. They do not feel that staff address this
effectively. School rules dictate that pupils cannot interact with their peers in other year
groups at social times. This includes their siblings. Staff expect pupils to eat in silence at
lunch and snack times and work silently in classrooms. This limits the development of
pupils’ social skills and their understanding of social norms and conventions. In some
instances, pupils with protected characteristics do not receive the support they require to
ensure that they are safe in school.

Some pupils can articulate their learning about fundamental British values, such as
democracy. They also demonstrate an awareness of having learned about different faiths
and cultures.

The proprietor has not ensured that the standards in this part are met.


Part 3. Welfare, health and safety of pupils
Safeguarding

Staff receive regular safeguarding training. The proprietor has implemented an electronic
system for reporting and recording concerns. The system shows evidence of largely timely
and sufficiently detailed recording. The school generally takes appropriate action to follow
up on concerns, including involving parents and carers. However, the chronology of
records for some pupils is not well organised, which means the school has not responded
promptly to ensure pupils’ safety and wellbeing. Most pupils say that they would report
concerns to a trusted adult, but some are unclear about who they would go to if they were
worried.

The safeguarding and child protection policy references current guidance and legislation. It
is available to view on the school’s website.

 While staff know the process that should be followed when visitors are in school, the

ask them to sign into the building or provide them with a visitor’s badge in line with the

Pupils behave well. They are clear about the school rules and expectations. However,

The proprietor has not established a formal arrangement for the storage and

The purpose of the inspection is to advise the Secretary of State for Education
about the school’s likely compliance with the independent school standards (ISS)
that are relevant to the material change that the school has applied to make.


Part 8. Quality of leadership in and management of schools
When we carry out material change inspections of independent schools, we report
on the school’s likely compliance with part 8 of the ISS first. Under part 8, the
proprietor is required to ensure that the school meets all of the ISS consistently.
The standard in part 8 is intended to ensure that the quality of leadership and
management at the school is sufficient for that purpose.

Leadership across the school is effective. The headteacher, who also operates as a
member of the proprietor body, and other leaders bring relevant expertise to the
school. Leaders use external sector experts, who have significant and broad-
ranging educational and wider expertise, to quality assure their work and to offer
support and challenge. Leaders demonstrate a secure understanding of the ISS
and take actions to ensure that they are met.

Current pupils feel safe and are happy in school. They trust staff, developing
positive and supportive relationships. Appropriate staff ratios mean that pupils are

 supported to develop and maintain effective relationships through tailored support.
Staff receive appropriate training so that they can undertake their roles well.

Leaders have made significant developments to the school site, taking on
additional premises, to provide for an increased number of pupils. These premises
are appropriately designed, furnished and safe and are well maintained. However,
the sites do not currently have sufficient space and resources for the full number
of proposed additional pupils. As a result, they are unlikely to meet the ISS if the
material change application is approved. However, these standards are more likely
to be met were a lower number of additional pupils to be requested.


Part 3. Welfare, health and safety of pupils
Safeguarding

The school’s safeguarding policy is published on the school’s website and aligns
with statutory requirements. Staff receive comprehensive safeguarding training
which is regularly updated, ensuring they can identify when a pupil may be at risk
of harm and report any concerns swiftly.

Leaders are appropriately trained for their roles in overseeing the safeguarding
culture in their school. Several leaders have appropriate training to perform the
role of designated safeguarding lead, ensuring that at least one is present at each
of the 3 sites at any time. Leaders work well with external agencies so that pupils
and their families receive appropriate and timely support. Records are kept of
actions undertaken, which are appropriately detailed and demonstrate that
responses are timely.

Health and safety, fire and first aid

The school has appropriate health and safety and first-aid policies in place that
support the welfare of pupils and staff. These policies are implemented
consistently and underpinned by effective systems. Leaders ensure that frequent
health and safety checks of the school site are carried out. Any identified
issues are addressed swiftly. As a result of these systems, the site is maintained to
a high standard and is safe. This includes the recently acquired third site that
leaders intend to be the base for the proposed increased numbers of pupils.

A compliant fire safety policy is in place. Across all 3 sites, clear escape routes are
supported by ample signage. Robust systems, including frequent checks of alarms,
fire extinguishers and emergency lighting are in place. Regular external checks are
undertaken of fire extinguishers to ensure these are well maintained. These
processes ensure the school maintains ongoing compliance with fire safety
regulations.

A thorough risk assessment policy is in place, supported by clear systems and
processes that are carefully followed. Risk assessments are well written, reflecting

Leaders have individual risk assessments in place that are reviewed frequently to

be met were a lower number of additional pupils to be requested.

Recruitment processes within the school are robust and give due regard to safer
recruitment requirements. The senior leaders involved in recruitment are

The school already has sufficient staff to meet the needs of the proposed
increased capacity, who they propose to train to deliver the curriculum. The school
has appropriate training and monitoring programmes in place to ensure that
all new staff are able to support pupils safely and effectively.

completed and recorded appropriately.

The safeguarding standards are met. This means that leaders and/or those responsible for

How we evaluate safeguarding


When we inspect schools for safeguarding, they can have the following outcomes:

  Met: The school has an open and positive culture of safeguarding. All legal requirements

  Not met: The school has not created an open and positive culture of safeguarding. Not all

 Strong standard

Early years                                                                   Strong standard

Children in the early years benefit from a language-rich, purposeful and inclusive learning
environment. The curriculum is well structured and clearly sequenced. Leaders ensure that
the curriculum is well taught. They make changes to improve provision as appropriate, for
example when focusing on developing communication skills.

Staff engage in high-quality interactions. Their expectations of the way that children
communicate and use appropriate vocabulary are high. During a mathematics session, for
example, the children presented their answers to number challenges in full sentences. The
provision for 2-year-olds is equally as effective. Children repeat key vocabulary while taking
part in the ‘scarf dance’.

Leaders ensure that relationships with parents and carers are highly positive. Staff work
quickly to get to know every child and their family well. Leaders and staff quickly and
accurately identify children who face barriers to their learning and wellbeing, providing swift,
effective support.

Highly effective routines and expectations are established. As a result, children feel safe,
behave well and make notable progress from their individual starting points.

Early reading, writing and number skills are taught effectively. Staff check learning carefully
so that children build their knowledge and develop their vocabulary. Children are well
prepared for Year 1.


Inclusion                                                                     Strong standard

Leaders are committed to meeting the needs of every pupil across all of the different
vulnerable groups. Pupils’ individual needs are identified and assessed effectively. Leaders
work with parents and carers and external agencies to reduce barriers to learning through
highly effective provision. This includes an array of adaptations that enable pupils to access
learning fully with their peers. As a result, pupils develop independence and have the skills
and knowledge to excel. Parents are overwhelmingly positive about the support that their
children receive.

Pupils who find learning the hardest benefit from high quality, inclusive teaching. This is
particularly evident with the work with the ‘acorns’ specialist provision and ‘ready, respectful,
safe’ group, where effectively tailored programmes support pupils to build the skills and
knowledge that they need to succeed.

Leaders have high aspirations for pupils with additional needs. They work effectively with
providers when pupils attend alternative provision. Leaders diligently monitor pupils’
progress and assess the impact of interventions and support strategies, including the impact
of the pupil premium funding. This thoughtful, proactive approach ensures that pupils who
face barriers to their learning and wellbeing are supported to achieve well.
 Staff benefit from a well-planned professional development programme. The training
supports them to understand pupils’ needs better.

Leaders have created a welcoming, purposeful and highly inclusive culture in the school.
They have an astute understanding of the priorities for development to ensure the best
possible outcomes and experiences for pupils. They take timely action to improve areas for
development, for example in ensuring that they get to know children from the earliest
opportunity with the development of the provision for 2-year-olds.

Leaders’ decisions are in the best interests of pupils, particularly those who face additional
barriers. Leaders want all pupils to succeed personally and academically. Leaders at all
levels invest in supporting all pupils to achieve well. The new headteacher has brought
direction and energy to the school. Staff and parents and carers are highly complimentary
about the effectiveness of the leadership team.

Leaders take thoughtful steps to support staff's workload and wellbeing. Leaders ensure that
staff feel valued. Staff appreciate how leaders support them to develop as professionals.

Governors carry out their statutory duties with diligence. They hold leaders to account and
maintain a clear focus on pupils’ needs. They know the school very well and value the
support from the trust.

Leaders, including those responsible for governance, forge highly effective relationships
beyond the school so that they can successfully engage with, and work in partnership with,
parents and the local community. They share good practice with other schools, for example
sharing the success of their ‘acorns’ provision. All parents who shared their views with
inspectors expressed confidence in the school and appreciate the strong relationships staff
build with their children.

Leaders have carefully considered the school's context when designing the well-sequenced
personal, social, health, and economic education curriculum. Leaders ensure that pupils
have the knowledge and skills for life beyond the primary school. They make sure that the
relationships, sex and health education is accessible to all pupils. This includes keeping
parents well informed of the content at an open coffee morning.

Pupils learn about the fundamental British values. They demonstrate a deep understanding
of respect and tolerance, and of the different cultures and faiths that make up their
community. They understand the importance of healthy relationships and how to keep
themselves safe when using social media. They demonstrate resilience, independence and

 Pupils are proud of their leadership roles. They talk about the importance of helping the

High-quality pastoral support means that pupils have the necessary skills to develop the

significantly on those who need it. Pupils are supported through responsive and planned
interventions, including sensory support and opportunities to manage their emotions. Pupils
with a range of needs receive consistently high-quality help that enables them to thrive.

Leaders meticulously track provision and adapt support when needed. They ensure that all
pupils access the broad and enticing offer.

curriculum areas, for example in history, errors in pupils' understanding are on occasion not
identified and corrected.

Teachers have detailed subject knowledge. They give clear instructions and take the time to
ensure that pupils understand what they are being asked to do. They adapt learning
successfully so that all pupils are fully included in the learning process.



What it's like to be a pupil at this school

Pupils and their families are valued parts of the Djanogly Strelley Academy family. Pupils
know that staff and leaders care about them. Pupils have a positive sense of belonging
where they feel that they are safe and are an integral part of the school community.

Pupils say that everyone is welcome in their school and that it is 'okay to be different'. They
say that ‘school is a great place to be’. As a result, many pupils attend well and attendance
is continuing to improve. Pupils engage with a well-planned, ambitious curriculum. They
enjoy their learning. They are keen to learn and make notable progress. Pupils, across all of
the vulnerable groups, thrive in a culture that supports them to ‘be the best that they can be’.

Pupils are well known by staff. As a result, staff quickly identify barriers to learning and
wellbeing for pupils and work together to reduce these barriers. Pupils in the ‘acorns’
specialist provision achieve well and get the bespoke support that they need.

Children in early years thrive. This begins when the youngest children, at the age of 2, start
school. They settle quickly and rise to the high expectations.
 Pupils enjoy enrichment activities, including clubs, trips and wider opportunities. This offer is
also extended to parents and carers, who benefit from coffee mornings and focused
sessions to help them to support their children.

Pupils rise to the high expectations of their behaviour. They behave well, showing respect
and care for one another. Bullying is rare, but when concerns arise, staff act swiftly to
provide the right support.

The older pupils support the younger ones through their leadership roles, including
safeguarding ambassadors and librarians. These roles help pupils to prepare to be a
positive members of the community.

   Safeguarding standards met

The safeguarding standards are met. This means that leaders and/or those responsible for
governance and oversight fulfil their specific responsibilities and have established an open
culture in which safeguarding is everyone's responsibility and concerns are actively
identified, acted upon and managed. As a result, pupils are made safer and feel safe.

How we evaluate safeguarding


When we inspect schools for safeguarding, they can have the following outcomes:

  Met: The school has an open and positive culture of safeguarding. All legal requirements
  are met.
  Not met: The school has not created an open and positive culture of safeguarding. Not all
  legal requirements are met.
  Insufficient evidence: Inspectors were unable to gather sufficient evidence to judge
  whether safeguarding standards are met.
 Expected standard

Achievement                                                                Expected standard

Pupils make steady progress from their starting points because leaders and staff understand
their needs and provide structured support. Many arrive with gaps in prior learning. The
school ensures that pupils receive effective support to help them build knowledge securely
over time. As a result, pupils gain confidence and show growing understanding across
subjects as they move through the school. Pupils are suitably prepared for their next steps
in education.

Pupils' achievement is most positive where teaching is well structured and revisits key skills
regularly, particularly in reading. A consistent phonics approach enables pupils to read
accurately, develop fluency and apply these skills independently. Pupils, including those who
are disadvantaged or have special educational needs and/or disabilities, generally make
positive progress because leaders reduce barriers and ensure they receive effective
support. Sometimes, when teaching does not use assessment with precision, some pupils'
depth of learning is limited.


Attendance and behaviour                                                   Expected standard

Leaders establish effective and well-embedded systems to promote pupils' attendance, and
this has a clear positive impact. Attendance remains high because leaders check and review
it daily. They follow up any pupils' absence promptly and maintain clear communication with
families. As a result, most pupils attend regularly. Leaders identify any concerns in pupils'
attendance quickly. They provide targeted support, including for pupils with additional needs,
which keeps persistent absence low. Careful management of transitions reflect leaders’
rigorous commitment to pupils’ welfare, stability and continuity in learning.

Leaders create an orderly and respectful environment where pupils feel safe, valued and
ready to learn. Positive relationships underpin this culture. Pupils behave well in lessons and
at social times. They respond to clear routines enthusiastically. Pupils concentrate well in
lessons, listen carefully, and participate actively in discussions. Staff apply the behaviour
policy consistently. This ensures that behavioural expectations remain high while support is
tailored effectively, allowing all pupils to succeed. Staff use positive reinforcement to
encourage high standards. Any serious behaviour incidents are rare and managed
effectively. This fosters a sense of safety and trust, enabling pupils to focus on their learning
without concern.


Curriculum and teaching                                                    Expected standard

Leaders have a clear and accurate understanding of strengths and priorities in the
curriculum and teaching. They take effective action to improve any areas that need
additional work. Recent developments in the structure of leadership have strengthened
focus and driven improvements. For instance, structured programmes in reading and
mathematics have led to consistent approaches across the school. Leaders’ focus on staff's
professional development strengthens teaching and supports the delivery of the intended
curriculum. Staff ensure that pupils develop secure foundations in their writing and
 mathematics. However, sometimes the precise use of assessment within lessons and in
some pupils' work lacks consistency. This reduces teachers’ ability to identify and address
misconceptions promptly. On occasion, higher-attaining pupils do not receive regular
challenge when they are ready for new content. This limits some pupils' depth of
understanding of key knowledge and vocabulary.

Leaders have designed an appropriate and increasingly coherent curriculum that equips
pupils with the knowledge and skills they need for their next stages of learning. For example,
pupils develop fluency, confidence and independence through a systematic phonics
programme, consistent teaching and well-matched resources. As a result, most pupils build
the skills they need to access learning successfully across the curriculum.


Inclusion                                                                Expected standard

Inclusion is a clear strength and is embedded at the heart of the school. Leaders
demonstrate a detailed and accurate understanding of individual pupils and their families.
Leaders prioritise the identification of pupils' needs. They ensure the timely use of baseline
assessments, ongoing reviews and clear recording systems. Leaders ensure that pupils,
including those who are disadvantaged, have special educational needs and/or disabilities
or those known or previously known to social care, receive prompt and appropriate support.
As a result, pupils feel known, supported and able to succeed in their learning. Staff support
and develop pupils' confidence, wellbeing and progress.

Leaders generally reduce barriers through suitable classroom practice, targeted support and
reasonable adjustments. Teaching strategies such as small-step learning, questioning and
scaffolding help pupils access the curriculum effectively. Targeted support helps regulate
pupils' behaviour and builds their independence. While information about pupils is detailed
and accessible, it is not sometimes used with sufficient precision to inform teaching. This
results in occasional variability in how effectively lessons are adapted and how well teaching
addresses gaps in pupils' learning.

Leaders track pupils' progress carefully through assessment, structured interventions and
review processes. This ensures that provision remains purposeful. Staff benefit from
focused training. Positive collaboration with families and external professionals enhances
consistency and impact for individual pupils well. Multi-agency work particularly supports
vulnerable pupils to succeed.


Leadership and governance                                                Expected standard

The proprietor and leaders provide clear and increasingly effective leadership. This has a
direct and positive impact on pupils’ experiences and outcomes. An unwavering vision
rooted in high expectations and care shapes the school’s work. The proprietor and leaders
foster practice that ensures everyone is treated fairly. Those responsible ensure that
everyone is given an equal chance to participate, be heard, and belong, as outlined in
Schedule 10 of the Equality Act 2010, Leaders ensure that pupils who face additional
barriers receive targeted support, enabling them to remain included in learning and make
steady progress. As a result, pupils learn in a supportive environment where they feel valued
and encouraged to succeed.
 Leaders understand the school’s strengths and priorities and take effective action to improve
provision. They have strengthened the curriculum, invested in staff development and
improved systems. This is leading to clear gains, especially in reading and inclusive
practice. The proprietor has secured important changes following previous challenges,
including strengthening leadership structures. Their reflective approach, combined with a
clear commitment to improvement, positions the school well to continue developing. Staff
benefit from focused professional learning opportunities and feel supported, which improves
teaching and consistency. Leaders manage staff workload carefully and maintain a positive
culture because leaders are approachable and mindful of staff's needs.

Leaders and managers are effective in meeting the independent school standards. All
required documentation is in place and fit for purpose. Despite some ongoing uncertainty
around the use of the premises in the future, the proprietor and leaders maintain a sharp
focus on ensuring that pupils continue to receive a safe and effective education.


Personal development and wellbeing                                       Expected standard

Leaders have designed a personal development programme that reflects the distinctive
context and values of the school. Through Kodesh, personal development lessons and daily
interactions, pupils reflect on their own beliefs and develop a clear understanding of right
and wrong. They respect others’ views and recognise that people may live differently or hold
different beliefs. Pupils talk confidently about respecting different family structures and
backgrounds. This prepares them well for life beyond the school while maintaining a strong
connection to their own identity and community.

Leaders work closely with parents and carers with regards to relationships and health
education. This includes consulting them on key content such as puberty, which builds trust
and ensures alignment with family values. Pupils learn how to stay safe both online and
offline, and leaders reinforce these messages regularly, recognising that pupils’ access to
technology can vary. When sensitive issues arise, staff respond with care and provide
individual guidance, ensuring that pupils feel supported and understood.

Leaders place importance on developing pupils’ character and resilience. Pupils are
encouraged to try their best because staff encourage them and support them to succeed.
Enrichment opportunities, including visits, practical activities such as design and technology
work, and many clubs, broaden pupils’ experiences and help them develop new interests.
These opportunities also provide important avenues for pupils, including those with special
educational needs, to experience success beyond the classroom.

There is a growing emphasis on preparing pupils for future pathways, including early
exposure to careers through planned visits and experiences. While this is developing, it
already helps pupils begin to understand the wider world and consider future possibilities in
a way that is appropriate to their age and context.
 What it's like to be a pupil at this school

Pupils enjoy learning and engage positively with the curriculum, which supports their
achievement over time. They speak enthusiastically about their lessons, particularly in
Jewish studies, mathematics and science, where practical tasks, discussion and real-life
connections deepen understanding. Pupils ask thoughtful questions and build on prior
knowledge, enabling steady progress across subjects. They develop secure reading skills
and use phonics to support spelling where appropriate.

Leaders and staff work deliberately to reduce any barriers to pupils' learning and wellbeing,
especially for disadvantaged pupils and those with special educational needs and/or
disabilities. Pupils who find learning more challenging learn alongside their peers and
develop resilience because staff consistently encourage them and celebrate their efforts and
improvements.

Pupils experience a deep sense of belonging within a close-knit, welcoming community
where everyone feels 'as one'. They are proud of their school and describe it as a happy
place. Relationships are positive here because pupils treat each other with kindness and
recognise that staff are approachable and committed to helping them succeed. This helps
pupils feel comfortable asking for help, sharing concerns and contributing ideas in lessons.

Pupils benefit from a range of wider opportunities, including design and technology projects,
chess, performances, visits and links with external settings such as a local special school.
These experiences broaden horizons, develop social skills and spark new interests for
pupils.

Pupils feel safe and trust staff, including when concerns arise beyond school. Behaviour is
positive because expectations are clear and understood. Pupils develop self-control and
take responsibility for their actions. Bullying is rare and dealt with promptly. Attendance is
high because pupils feel valued and enjoy coming to school. Through the curriculum and
wider experiences, pupils learn respect, responsibility and understanding of different beliefs,
preparing them well as thoughtful members of society.



Next steps

  Leaders should ensure that staff routinely check pupils’ understanding and promptly
  identify and address misconceptions in lessons and in pupils’ work, so that pupils develop
  secure and precise knowledge and skills and improve achievement over time.
  Leaders and those responsible for governance should continue to develop staff expertise
  so that staff use well‑matched adaptations and strategies precisely in lessons to reduce
  barriers to learning for all pupils, including those with special educational needs and/or
  disabilities.

professionals. This ensures learning is relevant to current community issues and supports
pupils' understanding of risk. A wide range of opportunities, including guest speakers and
educational visits, enrich pupils' experiences. Leaders ensure that pupils, including those
who are disadvantaged, are very well prepared for life beyond school.

Pupils gain a sense of belonging. For example, by celebrating 'Hetton heroes' they explore
achievements within the local community. Pupil voice strongly informs provision, for
example, through discussions about effective budgeting and online safety. Learning is
structured to deepen pupils' understanding as they move through the school. Weekly
assemblies promote equality and offer pupils the opportunity to reflect on important
messages about British values, such as democracy, individual freedom and the rule of law.
Pupils are articulate, respectful and reflective when discussing diversity, fairness and
difference. Scenario-based learning, visits to places of worship and lessons about healthy
relationships further strengthen pupils' understanding. The sex and relationships education
and health education is taught effectively, in an age-appropriate way.

Pastoral care is extremely well planned. A graduated approach to nurture, supported by
assessments and external referrals where needed, ensures pupils' emotional and mental
health needs are met exceptionally well.

Pupils benefit from a wide range of clubs, leadership roles, such as 'friends against bullying',
and enrichment opportunities. Leaders closely track participation in these to ensure that
everyone is included. As a result, pupils develop character, responsibility and confidence.
Overall, pupils are eminently well prepared for life in modern Britain.




Expected standard

Achievement                                                               Expected standard

Pupils generally achieve well, as reflected in the school's published outcomes. The number
of pupils achieving the expected standard in reading, writing and mathematics at the end of
key stage 2 is close to or above the national average. This includes disadvantaged pupils,
who achieve well overall. Leaders recognise that too few pupils reached the higher standard
in reading in 2025, and that progress in writing for some pupils could be better. They are
addressing these issues effectively.

Younger pupils learn to read accurately and fluently. This is reflected in the average
proportion of pupils achieving the expected standard in the Year 1 phonics screening check.
 The school's sharp focus on securing basic knowledge and recent changes to the English
curriculum rapidly closes gaps in pupils' learning. This enables pupils to apply their
knowledge and skills in other subjects and ensures that, across the wider curriculum, pupils
typically progress well.


Attendance and behaviour                                                   Expected standard

Leaders demonstrate an effective and proactive approach to promoting positive attendance
and behaviour, ensuring pupils are able to access learning effectively. Pupils' attendance is
broadly in line with the national average and improving. Leaders' meticulous analysis of
attendance is driving this improvement. They identify and address any barriers to
attendance promptly, for any particular vulnerable groups in the school. They use support
from external agencies effectively where needed and work closely with families to ensure
pupils continue to access learning when they are unable to attend, for example when pupils
from the UK Guild of Showmen are travelling. Leaders' monitoring systems are
comprehensive, and they review the impact of their actions to inform future decisions.

Pupils throughout the school meet the high expectations for behaviour, showing respect for
staff and each other. They engage well in lessons. Classrooms are calm and orderly, and
disruption is rare. Staff apply the school's behaviour-related policies consistently and fairly.
Pupils who struggle to manage strong emotions benefit from targeted sensory support that
enables them to regulate their behaviour and participate fully in learning. Staff deal with any
behaviour incidents or instances of unkindness quickly and effectively. Pupils move calmly
and sensibly around the school. There is a culture of community and acceptance in the
school, in which differences are celebrated. Leaders' strategies to improve behaviour are
effective, creating a safe, respectful environment and sustaining high standards of conduct
overall.


Curriculum and teaching                                                    Expected standard

Leaders have a clear and accurate understanding of the quality of the curriculum and
teaching. They evaluate provision, making thoughtful decisions to secure further
improvement. Leaders have designed an ambitious, broad and balanced curriculum, which
is coherently sequenced across all subjects to enable pupils to build knowledge over time.
For example, pupils use their knowledge of multiplication facts gained in Year 2 when
learning more complex mathematical processes in later years.

The building blocks for reading, writing and mathematics are prioritised. Skilful phonics
teaching ensures pupils gain the knowledge they need to read accurately. Where pupils
need to catch up, leaders provide timely support. Across the curriculum, teaching develops
pupils' spoken and written language effectively. Pupils typically gain the knowledge they
need to prepare them for the next stage of their education.

Teaching is generally effective. Ongoing training helps teachers to deliver targeted support
and use adapted resources to reduce barriers to learning for disadvantaged pupils and
those with special educational needs and/or disabilities. Teachers use a range of checks to
identify pupils' starting points, address misconceptions and correct errors. However, this is
not consistent across the school. Sometimes teachers do not make the necessary checks.
 Leaders are currently improving assessment practices to ensure that pupils build knowledge
consistently well in all subjects.


Early years                                                                 Expected standard

The early years provision is welcoming. The learning environment is purposeful and staff
support children's development effectively. Leaders work well with parents to get to know
children's individual needs. They carefully plan learning for each child, making the right
adjustments to support their progress.

The early years curriculum enables children to build strong foundations for later learning.
For example, children have ample opportunities to learn pre-writing skills such as mark
making. Staff assess children individually to ensure their knowledge is secure before
progressing to letter formation. The wider curriculum is thoughtfully developed, with key
vocabulary introduced for each area of learning. This helps children to be ready for Year 1.

Leaders have rightly identified weaknesses in pencil grip as children move from early years
into key stage 1, and have taken decisive action. The school's new handwriting curriculum is
showing impact, alongside a renewed and well-planned focus on developing fine and gross
motor skills. Children benefit from a wide range of activities that strengthen their core
stability and hand control, such as using modelling dough and tweezers.

Daily phonics sessions and story time ensure that children gain the knowledge they need for
early reading and develop an enjoyment of books. Staff prioritise children's communication
and language. Staff generally engage well with children, having supportive interactions with
them.


Inclusion                                                                   Expected standard

Leaders place inclusion at the heart of the school's work. They promote a culture of high
expectations for all pupils. Pupils' needs are identified and assessed promptly and
accurately. Leaders work closely with families, professionals and external agencies to
ensure that pupils are known well as individuals. This enables leaders to put appropriate
support in place quickly so that pupils feel safe, valued and ready to learn.

Inclusive practices used across the school include reasonable adjustments and thoughtful
adaptations that enable pupils to access the full curriculum alongside their peers. Pupils
benefit from an environment where differences are understood and respected. Leaders
monitor pupils' progress closely and evaluate the impact of their provision. This ensures that
the support pupils receive remains responsive and that pupils make progress from a range
of starting points.

Staff receive the right training to build provision in line with pupils' needs. Additional funding
is used purposefully to strengthen inclusion and improve outcomes. Leaders have effective
processes in place to review the impact of this, for example the pupil premium grant. The
specially resourced provision for pupils with special educational needs and/or disabilities, as
 well as alternative provision arrangements, are effective and promote pupils' successful
participation in school life.


Leadership and governance                                                  Expected standard

Leaders demonstrate high expectations. They evaluate the school's work accurately,
providing detailed reports to governors and trustees that support informed decision-making.
Since the last inspection, leaders have strengthened their oversight of the curriculum,
sharing expertise across the school and with the wider local authority.

Leaders have an accurate understanding of the school's strengths, and they act effectively
to address areas for development, with a particular focus on meeting the needs of
vulnerable pupils. They engage with external agencies to enhance the curriculum and pupils'
experiences. For example, leaders ensure that pupils from the UK Guild of Showmen
community access distance learning packs and temporary schools to bridge the education
gaps caused by travel.

The collaborative and supportive culture in the school helps staff to feel valued and involved
in leaders' vision. Professional development is carefully aligned to school priorities, including
highly effective support for early career teachers.

Governors provide effective support and challenge, asking probing questions, following up
actions rigorously and holding leaders to account. Governors understand the school's
strategic direction, work cohesively as a team and maintain a visible presence at the school.
They fulfil their statutory duties.

Leaders and governors alike understand the importance of getting it right for all pupils,
including those who are disadvantaged and face other barriers to learning and/or wellbeing.
They are reflective and accurately identify when improvement is needed. Leaders make
decisions that are rooted in pupils' best interests. They foster a reflective and ambitious
environment where pupils and staff can thrive.
 What it's like to be a pupil at this school

Pupils thrive at this school. In the early years, children settle quickly because they are well
supported by caring staff. This helps children to work well together as they learn about the
world around them. This culture of collaboration and curiosity continues to develop as pupils
progress through the school.

Overall, pupils achieve well and show enjoyment of learning. They speak positively about
their lessons and value the ambitious, well-sequenced curriculum. Teachers help pupils to
build knowledge over time and prepare them well for their next steps. Pupils who are
disadvantaged and those with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND) receive
effective support to learn alongside their peers. Any barriers to learning are identified early
and addressed thoughtfully. Pupils who attend 'The Den', the school's specially resourced
provision for pupils with SEND, benefit from specialised learning. This enables these pupils
to acquire the skills they need to make progress through the curriculum.

Most pupils attend school often and participate enthusiastically in the extensive range of
activities on offer, for example tennis and brass band tuition. Pupils and parents and carers
enjoy attending events throughout the year, such as coffee mornings and May Day
celebrations. Leaders plan meaningful opportunities for pupils to take on responsibilities,
such as serving as school counsellors or school ambassadors. These roles help pupils to
feel trusted and appreciated, while making an active contribution to the school community.
They prepare pupils well for later life.

Pupils generally show positive attitudes to learning and to one another. They understand the
expectations of their behaviour, so reminders from staff are rarely needed. A highly effective
pastoral care programme supports pupils' confidence, resilience and emotional wellbeing.
Bullying is rare, and pupils are confident that adults will act swiftly and effectively should any
concerns arise. This helps pupils to feel safe.

 What is it like to attend this school?

Abberley Parochial Primary School is at the heart of its community. Pupils and their
families are warmly welcomed to school each day. The school is ambitious for all pupils. It
sets high expectations for pupil achievement. Published outcomes confirm that pupils
achieve well. They enjoy attending. The school does all it can to ensure pupils attend
regularly and on time. The vast majority do. Parents and carers are extremely positive
about the quality of education their children receive.

The school is calm and orderly. Staff consistently provide clear routines and apply the
school’s high behaviour expectations. In classrooms, pupils listen attentively and engage
in the learning tasks set. They enjoy interactive lessons. This helps them to maintain
interest and focus. Pupil leaders organise age-appropriate activities and games during
‘happy playtimes’. Staff and the pupil well-being team are on hand to support and listen to
any worries or concerns pupils have. Pupils are well-mannered, polite and well-behaved.

Pupils say that the school is ‘an interesting, fun place to be’. They proudly take on
responsibilities in school, such as being eco-warriors, lunchtime buddies, online safety
leaders and librarians. Pupils value the worry boxes made available to them in school.
They make good use of them. Pupils feel happy and safe.

What does the school do well and what does it need to do better?

The school has adopted an ambitious curriculum for its pupils. The knowledge and skills
that pupils need to know are well sequenced with clear end points. Teachers have the
subject knowledge they need to teach the curriculum well. Pupils say lessons are
interesting and teachers help them to learn in fun ways, particularly in mathematics. Work
given to pupils helps them to apply their learning well. Pupils take great pride in their
work. Teachers make checks on learning in lessons and at regular intervals. They use this
information to plan next steps and address gaps in learning. All this means that pupils
achieve well in school. They learn and remember more of the school’s ambitious
curriculum.

Early reading is prioritised. Staff are highly skilled in delivering phonics lessons. Pupils
learn to blend sounds to read simple words and sentences. They apply newly learned
sounds when reading books that match these sounds. Pupils who fall behind are swiftly
identified. While they are well supported to catch up in their phonics knowledge, some
pupils do not get enough additional opportunities to practise their reading. This has an
impact on the speed at which they become confident, fluent readers.

Children in the early years get off to a great start. Learning is carefully planned by skilled
adults. It builds on what children know, understand and can do. Language and
communication are prioritised. Children develop an effective pencil grip and form letters
accurately. They investigate and hypothesise about how to free penguins frozen in the
water tray. Children enjoy finding out about Africa while creating pastel drawings of the
Savannah. They show the class rule of kindness by sharing and taking turns. All this
means children are well prepared for the next stage.

 The additional needs of pupils with special educational needs and or disabilities (SEND)
are swiftly identified. Pupils with SEND get the help and support they need to be
successful in school. Staff adapt learning to support pupils to access the curriculum.
External agencies provide specialist support such as speech and language therapy. Pupils
with SEND achieve well in school.

Pupils learn about the importance of places of worship to different faiths when visiting a
mosque, a church and a Hindu temple. This helps them to understand tolerance and
respect. Castle and museum trips, workshops, residentials and geography fieldwork
studies help pupils to deepen their knowledge of the curriculum. Hockey, football, ballet,
French and computing clubs offer opportunities to encourage new interests. The work of
the school council helps pupils to understand democracy. Pupils learn how to keep safe
online and offline. They learn about healthy and safe relationships. The school rules help
pupils to understand right and wrong, and they do. Pupils are respectful of others. The
school’s personal development offer provides a range of opportunities to broaden pupils’
horizons. However, there is work to do to strengthen this aspect of the school’s work so
that it is coherently planned and set out.

School leaders, including governors, set the right priorities for the school. Rigorous checks
on the progress of these priorities have brought about significant recent improvements.
Governors hold the headteacher to account effectively for the performance of the school.
In addition, the diocese and the local authority provide highly effective support and
challenge. The school is now moving forward at pace. Staff value support from leaders to
reduce workload and improve their well-being.

Safeguarding

The arrangements for safeguarding are effective.

What does the school need to do to improve?

(Information for the school and appropriate authority)

 Some pupils who have fallen behind in their reading do not get enough additional
  opportunities to practise reading. This has an impact on how quickly they become
  fluent, confident readers. The school should ensure pupils who need to catch up in
  their reading have regular and effective opportunities to practise reading so they read
  with the confidence and fluency expected for their age.
 Although broad, the school’s personal development offer is not coherently planned and
  set out. The purpose of the offer is unclear at times, as is its intended impact. The
  school should strengthen the personal development offer so it is coherently planned
  and its purpose is clearly set out.
